sub_units.name: Priority Queues and Heaps
sub_units.content: A heap is a specialized tree-based data structure satisfying the heap property. In a max heap, every node's value is greater than or equal to its children. In a min heap, every node's value is less than or equal to its children. Heaps power Priority Queues and are used for efficiently extracting min/max elements in O(log N) time.

questions.title: Min-Heap Property
questions.content: Which of the following correctly describes a Min-Heap?

mcq_options.text: For every node, its value is less than or equal to the values of its children.
For every node, its value is greater than or equal to the values of its children.
The tree must be a complete binary search tree.
The smallest element is always at a leaf node.

hints: Think about the definition of a heap property — does it apply to every parent-child pair, or just the root?
Compare min-heap and max-heap: in which one is the root the smallest element?
Remember: a heap is a complete binary tree, not necessarily a binary search tree.

questions.title: Heap Insert Time Complexity
questions.content: What is the time complexity of inserting an element into a binary heap of size N?
hints: When you insert into a heap, where does the new element go first?
After placing the element at the end, you may need to 'bubble up' to restore the heap property. How many levels can you bubble up?
The height of a complete binary tree with N nodes is O(log N).

questions.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.content:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array.

Note: it is the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct element.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: After sorting in descending order: [6,5,4,3,2,1]. The 2nd largest is 5.

questions.inputFormat:
The first line contains the integer array nums as a JSON list.
The second line contains the integer k.
questions.outputFormat: A single integer, the kth largest element.

solutions.title: Brute Force - Sorting
solutions.code:
import sys
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
nums = eval(input_data[0])
k = int(input_data[1])
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums[k-1])
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N) for sorting. Space: O(1). Logic: Sorting the entire array and picking the Kth element is the simplest approach.

solutions.title: Optimized - Min Heap of Size K
solutions.code:
import sys, heapq
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
nums = eval(input_data[0])
k = int(input_data[1])
heap = []
for num in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, num)
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)
print(heap[0])
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K). Logic: A Min-Heap of size K maintains the K largest elements. The smallest among these K is the Kth largest element overall.

solutions.title: Sorting - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(1). Simple sorting approach picking the Kth element from the end.

solutions.title: Min Heap - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K).

solutions.title: Sorting - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(1).

solutions.title: Min Heap - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K).

solutions.title: Sorting - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N).

solutions.title: Min Heap - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K).

hints: Sorting the array would place the Kth largest element at index N-K. Can we do better than O(N log N)?
A Min-Heap of size K can track the K largest elements seen so far. The smallest among these is the Kth largest.
Iterate through the array, pushing elements into the heap. If the heap size exceeds K, pop the smallest element. The final top of the heap is your answer.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.content:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- k is in the range [1, the number of unique elements in the array]
- The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times and 2 appears 2 times. They are the 2 most frequent.

questions.inputFormat:
The first line contains the integer array nums as a JSON list.
The second line contains the integer k.
questions.outputFormat: A sorted list of the k most frequent elements.

solutions.title: Brute Force - Sort by Frequency
solutions.code:
import sys
from collections import Counter
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
nums = eval(input_data[0])
k = int(input_data[1])
count = Counter(nums)
sorted_items = sorted(count.keys(), key=lambda x: count[x], reverse=True)
print(sorted(sorted_items[:k]))
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N) for sorting unique elements. Space: O(N). Logic: Counting frequencies and then sorting all unique elements based on those frequencies.

solutions.title: Optimized - Bucket Sort
solutions.code:
import sys
from collections import Counter
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
nums = eval(input_data[0])
k = int(input_data[1])
count = Counter(nums)
buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
for num, freq in count.items():
    buckets[freq].append(num)
result = []
for i in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
    for num in buckets[i]:
        result.append(num)
        if len(result) == k:
            print(sorted(result))
            exit()
print(sorted(result))
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(N). Logic: Using frequencies as indices in a bucket array allows us to retrieve top elements in linear time.

solutions.title: Sort by Frequency - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Counting frequencies in a HashMap and then sorting the keys results in a clean O(N log N) solution.

solutions.title: Bucket Sort - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(N). Logic: Bucket sort allows linear time frequency tracking by using counts as array indices.

solutions.title: Sort by Frequency - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: C++ implementation using a map for counting and a vector for sorting by frequency.

solutions.title: Bucket Sort - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(N). Logic: Using bucket sort in C++ to achieve O(N) complexity for frequency-based retrieval.

solutions.title: Sort by Frequency - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N^2) for counting + O(N log N) for sorting. Space: O(N). Logic: Manual frequency counting and sorting in C.

solutions.title: Min Heap - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K) using a Min-Heap of size K. Space: O(N). Logic: Efficient frequency tracking using a heap.

hints: First, you need to count the frequency of each element. A HashMap or Counter would be perfect for this.
How can you use the frequencies to find the top K elements? Sorting the unique elements by frequency would take O(N log N).
Can we use a Min-Heap of size K to maintain the top frequencies? Or perhaps Bucket Sort for an O(N) solution?

questions.title: Last Stone Weight
questions.content:
You are given an array of integers stones where stones[i] is the weight of the ith stone.

We are playing a game with the stones. On each turn, we choose the heaviest two stones and smash them together. Suppose the heaviest two stones have weights x and y with x <= y:
- If x == y, both stones are destroyed.
- If x != y, the stone of weight x is destroyed, and the stone of weight y has new weight y - x.

At the end of the game, there is at most one stone left. Return the weight of the last remaining stone. If there are no stones left, return 0.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= stones.length <= 30
- 1 <= stones[i] <= 1000

solutions.title: Max Heap - Python
solutions.code:
import sys, heapq
stones = eval(sys.stdin.read().strip())
heap = [-s for s in stones]
heapq.heapify(heap)
while len(heap) > 1:
    y = -heapq.heappop(heap)
    x = -heapq.heappop(heap)
    if y != x:
        heapq.heappush(heap, -(y - x))
print(-heap[0] if heap else 0)
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: A Max-Heap allows us to always extract the two heaviest stones in log(N) time.

solutions.title: Max Heap - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: PriorityQueue in Java acts as a Max-Heap (when reversed) to track the heaviest stones.

solutions.title: Max Heap - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Using std::priority_queue to simulate the stone smashing game.

solutions.title: Max Heap - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Manual Max-Heap implementation in C for efficient extraction and re-insertion.

hints: The problem asks you to repeatedly pick the TWO heaviest stones. Which data structure helps you find the max elements efficiently?
A Max-Heap is perfect here. You can insert all weights, then pop the two largest.
After smashing them, if there's a remainder, push it back into the heap. Continue until one or zero stones remain.

questions.title: Task Scheduler
questions.content:
Given a characters array tasks, representing the tasks a CPU needs to do, where each letter represents a different task. Tasks could be done in any order. Each task is done in one unit of time. For each unit of time, the CPU could complete either one task or just be idle.

However, there is a non-negative integer n that represents the cooldown period between two same tasks. There must be at least n units of time between any two same tasks.

Return the least number of units of times that the CPU will take to finish all the given tasks.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= tasks.length <= 10^4
- tasks[i] is upper-case English letter
- 0 <= n <= 100

solutions.title: Greedy Formula - Python
solutions.code:
import sys
from collections import Counter
lines = sys.stdin.read().strip().split('\n')
tasks = eval(lines[0])
n = int(lines[1])
count = Counter(tasks)
max_freq = max(count.values())
max_count = sum(1 for v in count.values() if v == max_freq)
result = max(len(tasks), (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + max_count)
print(result)
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(1). Logic: The total time is dictated by the highest frequency task and the cooling period. The formula calculates the minimum 'slots' needed, accounting for tasks with the same max frequency.

solutions.title: Greedy Formula - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(1). Logic: Greedy approach using a frequency array to determine cooling slots.

solutions.title: Greedy Formula - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(1). Logic: Standard Java implementation of the greedy math formula for task scheduling.

solutions.title: Greedy Formula - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(1). Logic: Efficient greedy scheduling using frequency counting in C++.

hints: The cooling period 'n' implies that if you have multiple tasks of the same type, you must wait 'n' intervals between them.
Prioritize the tasks with the highest frequency. Why? Because they are the most likely to cause idle time.
The formula (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + max_count gives the total time. Compare this with the total number of tasks.

questions.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
questions.content:
You are given an array of k linked-lists lists, each linked-list is sorted in ascending order.

Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it.

**Constraints:**
- k == lists.length
- 0 <= k <= 10^4
- 0 <= lists[i].length <= 500
- -10^4 <= lists[i][j] <= 10^4

solutions.title: Min Heap - Python
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K) where N is total elements, K is number of lists. Space: O(K). Logic: A Min-Heap of size K tracks the smallest current element from each list, allowing us to merge them in optimal time.

solutions.title: Min Heap - C
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(N) to store lists + O(K) for heap. Logic: Manual Min-Heap implementation in C for multi-way merge.

solutions.title: Min Heap - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(N). Logic: Using PriorityQueue in Java to efficiently merge K sorted streams.

hints: Imagine you have just two sorted lists. You could use two pointers. How does this scale to K lists?
At any moment, you only care about the smallest element among the current heads of the K lists.
A Min-Heap of size K can efficiently give you the minimum among K heads. Repeatedly pop the minimum and push the next element from the same list.

questions.title: Find Median from Data Stream
questions.content:
The median is the middle value in an ordered integer list. If the size of the list is even, there is no middle value, and the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Implement the MedianFinder class:
- MedianFinder() initializes the MedianFinder object.
- void addNum(int num) adds the integer num to the data structure.
- double findMedian() returns the median of all elements so far.

**Constraints:**
- -10^5 <= num <= 10^5
- There will be at least one element before calling findMedian.

solutions.title: Two Heaps - Python
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(log N) per add. O(1) for median. Space: O(N). Logic: Two heaps maintain the split point of the data. Small half is in Max-Heap, large half in Min-Heap.

solutions.title: Two Heaps - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(log N) per add. Space: O(N). Logic: Using PriorityQueue in Java to implement the two-heap median finding algorithm.

hints: Tracking the median in a sorted list is easy, but inserting into a sorted list takes O(N). Can we do better?
The median divides the data into two halves. Can we use two heaps to store these halves?
Use a Max-Heap for the smaller half and a Min-Heap for the larger half. Keep their sizes balanced (difference <= 1).

questions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.content:
You are given an array of integers nums, there is a sliding window of size k which is moving from the very left of the array to the very right. You can only see the k numbers in the window. Each time the sliding window moves right by one position.

Return the max sliding window.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
- 1 <= k <= nums.length

solutions.title: Monotonic Deque - Python
solutions.code:
import sys, json
from collections import deque
lines = sys.stdin.read().strip().split('\n')
nums = json.loads(lines[0])
k = int(lines[1])
dq = deque()
result = []
for i, n in enumerate(nums):
    while dq and dq[0] < i - k + 1:
        dq.popleft()
    while dq and nums[dq[-1]] < n:
        dq.pop()
    dq.append(i)
    if i >= k - 1:
        result.append(nums[dq[0]])
print(result)
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(K). Logic: A monotonic deque stores indices of potentials maximums. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, leading to linear time complexity.

solutions.title: Monotonic Deque - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(K). Logic: Java implementation using ArrayDeque to maintain maximums in O(1) amortized time per slide.

solutions.title: Monotonic Deque - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N). Space: O(K). Logic: Using std::deque in C++ for an efficient monotonic sliding window maximum solver.

hints: A brute-force solution checking each window takes O(N * K). Can we optimize this with a deque or heap?
We need to quickly find the maximum in the window. A monotonic deque can store indices of elements in decreasing order.
As the window slides, remove indices that are out of bounds and elements smaller than the current one from the back of the deque. The front will always be the max.

questions.title: K Closest Points to Origin
questions.content:
Given an array of points where points[i] = [xi, yi] represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer k, return the k closest points to the origin (0, 0).

The distance between two points on the X-Y plane is the Euclidean distance (√(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2).

You may return the answer in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique (except for the order that it is in).

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= k <= points.length <= 10^4
- -10^4 <= xi, yi <= 10^4

solutions.title: Max Heap - Python
solutions.code:
import sys, heapq, json
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
points = json.loads(input_data[0])
k = int(input_data[1])
heap = []
for x, y in points:
    dist = -(x*x + y*y)
    if len(heap) == k:
        heapq.heappushpop(heap, (dist, x, y))
    else:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (dist, x, y))
res = [[x, y] for d, x, y in heap]
# Sort by distance (descending heap was used, but res is now distance squared)
# To match test cases, we sort by distance squared, then by x, then by y
print(json.dumps(sorted(res, key=lambda p: (p[0]**2 + p[1]**2, p[0], p[1]))))
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K). Logic: A Max-Heap of size K stores the closest points. Using squared distance (x^2 + y^2) avoids expensive square root calculations.

solutions.title: Sorting - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N) for full sort, though O(N log K) is possible with a heap. Space: O(N). Logic: Sorting all points by distance and taking the first K.

solutions.title: Sorting - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: C++ implementation using sorting based on Euclidean distance squared.

hints: The distance to the origin is sqrt(x^2 + y^2). For comparison, x^2 + y^2 is sufficient and more efficient.
Sorting all points by distance takes O(N log N). Can we use a heap to maintain only the K closest ones in O(N log K)?
A Max-Heap of size K can store the closest points seen so far. If a new point is closer than the current farthest in the heap, replace it.

questions.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
questions.content:
You have some sticks with positive integer lengths. You can connect any two sticks of lengths x and y into one stick by paying a cost of x + y. You perform this action until there is one stick remaining.

Return the minimum cost to connect all the given sticks into one stick.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= sticks.length <= 10^4
- 1 <= sticks[i] <= 10^4

solutions.title: Min Heap - Python
solutions.code:
import sys, heapq, json
sticks = json.loads(sys.stdin.read().strip())
if len(sticks) < 2: print(0); exit()
heapq.heapify(sticks)
cost = 0
while len(sticks) > 1:
    a = heapq.heappop(sticks)
    b = heapq.heappop(sticks)
    cost += a + b
    heapq.heappush(sticks, a + b)
print(cost)
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: This is a greedy problem where we always connect the two shortest sticks. A Min-Heap allows us to find and combine the shortest sticks efficiently.

solutions.title: Min Heap - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Java PriorityQueue used as a Min-Heap to find the smallest lengths at each step.

solutions.title: Min Heap - C++
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(N log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Greedy stick connection strategy implemented in C++ with priority_queue.

hints: This problem is about combining elements to minimize total cost. Which pair should you combine at each step?
Combining the two shortest sticks is always greedy-optimal. Their sum will be part of future connection costs.
A Min-Heap can keep the stick lengths sorted. Pop the two smallest, push their sum, and repeat until one stick remains.

questions.title: Smallest Number in Infinite Set
questions.content:
You have a set which contains all positive integers [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ...].

Implement the SmallestInfiniteSet class:
- SmallestInfiniteSet() Initializes the SmallestInfiniteSet object to contain all positive integers.
- int popSmallest() Removes and returns the smallest integer contained in the infinite set.
- void addBack(int num) Adds a positive integer num back into the infinite set, if it is not already in the infinite set.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= num <= 1000
- At most 1000 calls will be made in total to popSmallest and addBack.

solutions.title: Min Heap + Set - Python
solutions.code:
import sys, heapq, json
input_data = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
ops = json.loads(input_data[0])
args = json.loads(input_data[1])
curr = 1
added = []
added_set = set()
res = []
for op, arg in zip(ops, args):
    if op == "SmallestInfiniteSet": res.append(None)
    elif op == "popSmallest":
        if added:
            val = heapq.heappop(added)
            added_set.remove(val)
            res.append(val)
        else:
            res.append(curr)
            curr += 1
    elif op == "addBack":
        num = arg[0]
        if num < curr and num not in added_set:
            heapq.heappush(added, num)
            added_set.add(num)
        res.append(None)
print(json.dumps(res).replace("null", "null"))
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(log N) per operation. Space: O(N). Logic: We use a counter for the 'infinite' part and a Min-Heap + Set for numbers that are added back. This keeps operations efficient.

solutions.title: Min Heap - Java
solutions.complexity_analysis: Time: O(log N). Space: O(N). Logic: Java implementation using PriorityQueue and HashSet to track the smallest available numbers.

hints: The 'infinite' part suggests we shouldn't actually store all positive integers. We only need to track the ones removed or added back.
Use a counter to track the smallest integer that hasn't been 'touched' yet.
A Min-Heap combined with a set can track 'added back' integers that are smaller than our current counter.
